title: kv-cache-pressure-sim-results-wip
content:
TL;DR:
We ran a set of synthetic pressure simulations to understand how cache reuse rates, eviction policy sensitivity, and host memory bandwidth interact under different request mixes. Key findings:
- High temporal locality (Zipf skew ~0.9) yields >85% KV reuse and stable p95 latency; naive LRU works fine.
- Under moderate skew (Zipf 0.6) reuse drops to ~55% and eviction churn causes frequent host->GPU page transfers; observed ~18% increase in p95 latency and 12% token/sec throughput drop.
- When memory bandwidth (NUMA node -> GPU DMA) is the bottleneck, reducing prefetch/debounce aggression (i.e., delay eviction-induced DMA) improves tail latency though lowers instantaneous throughput.
- Segmented LRU (hot/cold) reduced cold eviction churn by ~30% in our simulated chat-heavy workload and improved effective hit ratio by 6–9%.

Experiment notes / motivation:
We see production incidents where latency suddenly regresses during bursty churn (customer A, chatbot). Hypothesis: the KV cache sees working set spikes that exceed the cache footprint; eviction causes a wave of host->GPU transfers which hits PCIe/DRAM bandwidth and increases tail latency. The goal here is to reproduce and measure the cascade and validate mitigations (policy tuning, prefetch backoff, tightened key collocation).

Environment & baseline:
- Runtime: local dev cluster sim image of runtime v0.38.3 (feature flags: kv-prefetch=false, eviction-slowdown=false).
- Hardware used: 1x A100-40GB (PCIe link), host: 2x AMD EPYC 7H12, 512GB DRAM.
- OS: Ubuntu 22.04, CUDA 12.2.
- Prof tools: perf (5.10), nvprof / nv-nsight for GPU copy timelines, iostat, sar, nethogs (for completeness), and a tiny shim that logs DMA start/end per request (instrumented in runtime).

Workloads synthesized:
1) Zipf-heavy-chat: request mix = 70% short chat messages (prefix length mean 64 tokens), 30% long (512+), Zipf parameter 0.9 -> strong reuse of recent prefixes.
2) Uniform-completion: uniformly random new prompts, mostly long sequences (1024 tokens), simulating model-exploration/bench.
3) Mixed-burst: bursts of 500 concurrent sessions each with random prefix reuse (zipf 0.6), interleaved with background inference at 10% capacity.

Cache config parameters tested:
- Cache size: 6GB/12GB/20GB on host (affects how many KV shards resident).
- Eviction policy: LRU, segmented-LRU (hot/cold), TTL-based (workshop prototype).
- Eviction throttle: immediate vs debounce 50–200ms (experimental).
- Preload/prefetch: aggressive (transfer on partial prefix touch) vs lazy (transfer on first GPU query).

Measurement methodology:
- Metrics: KV hit ratio (per-key), token/sec throughput, p50/p95/p99 latency for token generation, host->gpu DMA bandwidth utilization (sampled per-second), CPU runqueue, GPU %util for kernels, and DMA concurrency.
- Each run: warmup 2m, measurement 5m, cool-down 1m. Repeated 3x and median taken.
- All runs executed with identical random seeds where applicable and logged in experiment-control repo.

Representative results (selected):
1) Zipf-heavy-chat, cache 12GB, LRU:
- KV hit ratio: 0.87
- Token/sec: 42k
- p95 token latency: 72ms
- Observed DMA spikes: occasional, but single large DMA only when very long prefix appears
- Notes: stable, low eviction churn.

2) Mixed-burst, cache 12GB, LRU:
- KV hit ratio: 0.56
- Token/sec: 36.8k (12% drop vs Zipf-heavy)
- p95 token latency: 85ms (18% increase)
- DMA bandwidth: sustained 68% of PCIe/DRAM link for ~15s windows during bursts, correlated with eviction waves
- CPU runqueue: increased context switching during DMA completion callbacks

3) Mixed-burst, cache 12GB, segmented-LRU (2-segment hot/cold threshold 8 accesses):
- KV hit ratio: 0.62 (effective by keeping hot keys pinned longer)
- Token/sec: 38.6k
- p95 token latency: 78ms
- DMA bandwidth peaks dampened by ~30%
- Notes: segmented LRU successfully reduced churn; overhead of a small extra metadata update per hit was negligible (<2% CPU).

4) Mixed-burst, cache 6GB, LRU, debounce 200ms:
- KV hit ratio: 0.49
- Token/sec: 34.1k
- p95: 92ms (worse)
- Observations: Debounce reduced instantaneous parallel DMAs but caused more cold misses overall; net effect worse in this mixed workload.

Profiling outputs & diagnostics collected:
- nv-nsight timeline: shows bursts of cudaMemcpyAsync events aligning to eviction windows; peak concurrent transfers = 6; average transfer size per request ~18MB (dependent on model kv shard size).
- perf stat: context-switches and page-faults rose ~3x during eviction waves.
- Runtime logs: eviction queue length spikes preceding p95 increases; shuffle of keys between host pages logged with monotonically increasing LRU-update latency for high-concurrency.
- Host DRAM read bandwidth (measured via sar and custom membench): peaked at ~22GB/s during the worst windows; our PCIe link saturates at ~12–14GB/s observed for DMA (matches device counters).

Analysis / hypotheses validated:
1) Hot/cold segmentation reduces frequent evict/restore cycles by keeping high-frequency keys resident; particularly effective when working set has a small hot subset.
2) Debounce (throttling immediate re-fetches) helps only when bandwidth is the dominant bottleneck and the workload has a significant proportion of later reuses (i.e., not too many one-off keys). In mixed-burst we had too many one-off keys so debounce was net negative.
3) The real problem is simultaneous large transfers from multiple evictions; reducing concurrent DMAs (serialize to N parallel transfers) reduces p95 at the cost of peak throughput. This is a tunable knob depending on SLOs.

Potential mitigations to try next (prioritized):
- Implement segmented-LRU as an opt-in policy in runtime and enable for chat workloads; add a small per-key hot-score decay with config knob. (high priority)
- Add a DMA concurrency limiter (configurable parallelism, default 3) that throttles prefetch when bandwidth > threshold. (medium)
- Introduce lightweight key sampling to detect when working set has high uniqueness; auto-switch to TTL or cold-first eviction to avoid chasey re-inserts. (medium)
- Improved telemetry: add rolling histogram for DMA size and per-request eviction cost in traces to drive smarter rollouts. (low)

Open questions / unknowns:
- How will segmented-LRU interact with quantized KV sharding (variable shard sizes)? Need to ensure hot promotion doesn't skew memory placement badly.
- Interaction with multi-tenant dedicated nodes — do we need tenant-aware quotas for eviction to avoid noisy neighbors?
- Cost model: what is the CPU overhead of maintaining per-key hot counters at 10k QPS? Benchmarks show ~1.5% CPU on our testbed but need wider validation.

Immediate action items:
- Diego: prototype segmented-LRU implementation branch and smoke tests (ETA 1w) -> github:pr/56
- Aisha: add per-request DMA logging into tracing pipeline and a Grafana panel for DMA size / concurrency (ETA 6d)
- Jonah: run same mixed-burst profile on a 2xA100 node (NVLink) to understand effect of higher interconnect bandwidth (ETA 10d)

Notes to keep: production incidents often have subtle compounding factors (concurrent large prompts + sudden user spike). Any mitigation must be able to be toggled by runtime routing policy (e.g., per-customer policy to prefer throughput vs tail).

Appendix: quick commands used (for reproducibility)
- start bench harness:
  PYTHONPATH=./bench python bench/run.py --profile mixed-burst --clients 500 --seed 42
- sample perf line:
  perf stat -e context-switches,cpu-migrations,page-faults -I 1000 -p <runtime_pid>
- collect nv-nsight timeline (headless):
  nsys profile --trace=cuda,cuda_memory,osrt -o /tmp/trace ./bin/runtime --bench-mode
- simple membandwidth spot check:
  sudo ./memcopy-bench --size 64M --iters 1000 --num-threads 4

If you want to pick a small follow-up, I recommend we land segmented-LRU as feature-flagged and add a simple DMA-concurrency limiter. Both are small isolated changes and should give immediate reduction in p95 during churn.

-- Maya
